description: Creating, inspecting and geometrically or arithmetically manipulating Image objects: dimensions, data extraction, resizing, cropping, rotation, padding, color space conversion, channel handling and image arithmetic. These are the foundation for all higher-level image processing in the Wolfram Language.

tools.name: Image
tools.description: Constructs an Image object from a numeric array, a list of channels, or another graphic. The array can be grayscale (rank 2) or multi-channel (rank 3), and the data type is controlled with the "type" argument. Images display inline and are accepted by every image-processing function.
tools.notes: Image[graphic] rasterizes graphics; use Rasterize for finer control over resolution.

tools.name: ImageDimensions
tools.description: Returns the pixel dimensions of an image as {width, height}. Note that this is the opposite order from the row/column dimensions of the underlying array. Use it before cropping, padding or resizing.

tools.name: ImageData
tools.description: Extracts the raw pixel values of an image as a nested list, with the first index running over rows from the top. A type argument converts values, for example "Byte" for 0-255 integers. Use it to move between images and ordinary array computations.
tools.notes: ImageData can be slow for large images; consider ImageApply or ImageMeasurements to stay inside the image system.

tools.name: ImageResize
tools.description: Resamples an image to a new size given as width, {width, height} or a scaled factor. Automatic in one slot preserves the aspect ratio. Several resampling methods are available, from nearest-neighbour to Lanczos.
tools.usage:
ImageResize[image, w]
ImageResize[image, {w, h}]
ImageResize[image, Scaled[s]]
tools.notes: Thumbnail is a convenient wrapper for making small previews; ImageResize with UpTo[n] bounds the larger dimension.

tools.name: ImageCrop
tools.description: Trims an image to a given size or removes uniform borders automatically. With a size it crops around the center by default, and a third argument selects which side to keep. Use it to standardize image sizes before batch processing.
tools.usage:
ImageCrop[image]
ImageCrop[image, {w, h}]
ImageCrop[image, {w, h}, Left]
tools.notes: ImageTake selects explicit row and column ranges; ImageTrim cuts out a region given by coordinates or a mask.

tools.name: ImageTake
tools.description: Extracts a rectangular block of rows and columns from an image, using the same index conventions as Take. Negative indices count from the far edge. Use it for precise sub-image extraction when you know pixel coordinates.

tools.name: ImageTrim
tools.description: Extracts the part of an image inside a specified region, given as corner points, a polygon, a disk or a mask. Unlike ImageTake it works in image coordinates with the origin at the bottom left. Use it to isolate detected objects returned as bounding boxes.

tools.name: ImageRotate
tools.description: Rotates an image by a given angle or by a named quarter-turn such as Right or Bottom. The canvas is enlarged to fit by default, or kept fixed with the "fit" argument. Padding and resampling methods are configurable.
tools.example:
img = ExampleData[{"TestImage", "House"}];
ImageRotate[img, 15 Degree, Full, Padding -> White]

tools.name: ImageReflect
tools.description: Flips an image about a horizontal, vertical or diagonal axis. Side specifications such as Left -> Right define the reflection. It is a fast, lossless operation often used for data augmentation.
tools.usage:
ImageReflect[image]
ImageReflect[image, side]
ImageReflect[image, s1 -> s2]
tools.example:
img = ExampleData[{"TestImage", "Lena"}];
{ImageReflect[img, Left -> Right], ImageReflect[img, Top -> Bottom]}

tools.name: ImagePad
tools.description: Adds or removes a border of given width around an image, filling it with a constant color or an extension of the image content. Negative widths crop instead of pad. Padding is essential before convolution to avoid edge artifacts.
tools.usage:
ImagePad[image, m]
ImagePad[image, {{l, r}, {b, t}}, padding]

tools.name: ImageTransformation
tools.description: Applies an arbitrary coordinate transformation to an image by inverse-mapping each output pixel. It handles warping, perspective correction and lens distortion models. Supply the function mapping output coordinates back to input coordinates.
tools.notes: For simple affine maps, ImageForwardTransformation or ImageRotate/ImageResize are faster.

tools.name: ImageAdjust
tools.description: Rescales image intensities to fill the full dynamic range, or adjusts brightness, contrast and gamma with explicit parameters. Called with just an image it performs a useful automatic stretch. Use it as a first step when an image looks flat or dark.
tools.usage:
ImageAdjust[image]
ImageAdjust[image, {contrast, brightness}]
ImageAdjust[image, {c, b, gamma}]
tools.notes: HistogramTransform gives histogram equalization, which often works better for low-contrast scientific images.

tools.name: HistogramTransform
tools.description: Transforms image intensities so their histogram matches a target distribution, uniform by default. This performs histogram equalization and, with a reference image, histogram matching. Use it to normalize illumination across a set of images.
tools.notes: HistogramTransformInterpolation gives a smoother, less blocky variant.

tools.name: ImageLevels
tools.description: Returns the histogram of pixel values in an image as a list of {value, count} pairs, per channel. It is the numeric counterpart of ImageHistogram. Use it to compute thresholds, check exposure or detect clipping.

tools.name: ImageHistogram
tools.description: Plots the distribution of pixel values in an image, with one overlaid curve or bar set per color channel. It accepts the usual Histogram options for bins and scaling. Use it to diagnose exposure, contrast and color casts.
tools.example:
img = ExampleData[{"TestImage", "Mandrill"}];
ImageHistogram[img, Automatic, "PDF", Frame -> True]

tools.name: ColorConvert
tools.description: Converts an image or color between color spaces such as RGB, grayscale, CMYK, LAB, HSB and XYZ. Converting to "Grayscale" is the standard preprocessing step for many analysis functions. It also works on individual color directives.
tools.notes: Some operations such as Binarize convert to grayscale automatically.

tools.name: ColorNegate
tools.description: Inverts the colors of an image or a color directive, mapping each channel value v to 1 - v. On binary masks it swaps foreground and background. It is frequently used before morphological operations that assume white objects.

tools.name: Binarize
tools.description: Converts an image to black and white using a global threshold, chosen automatically by Otsu's method if not given. A range keeps only values inside an interval. It is the usual first step before component analysis.
tools.notes: For uneven illumination use LocalAdaptiveBinarize or MorphologicalBinarize instead of a single global threshold.

tools.name: ImageAdd
tools.description: Adds images, numbers or colors pixel by pixel, clipping to the image's value range. All arguments must have compatible dimensions. Use it for brightening, compositing and accumulating frames.

tools.name: ImageSubtract
tools.description: Subtracts an image, number or color from an image, clipping negative results to zero. It is the standard way to remove a background frame or compute a difference image. Use ImageDifference for a symmetric absolute difference.

tools.name: ImageMultiply
tools.description: Multiplies images pixel by pixel, or scales an image by a number or color. Multiplying by a binary mask is the standard way to apply a region of interest. Values are clipped to the valid range.

tools.name: ImageDifference
tools.description: Computes the absolute difference between two images channel by channel. It is symmetric, unlike ImageSubtract, and is the usual tool for change detection and registration checks. Combine with ImageAdjust to make small differences visible.

tools.name: ImageApply
tools.description: Applies a function to the channel values of every pixel, receiving a list of channel values and returning new ones. It is the general per-pixel transformation tool. For neighborhood operations use ImageFilter instead.
tools.notes: ImageApplyIndexed passes the pixel position as well, which is useful for gradients and vignettes.

tools.name: ImageAssemble
tools.description: Joins a list or array of images into a single image, laying them out in rows and columns. All images in a row must share a height and all in a column a width, unless resizing options are given. Use it to build contact sheets and montages.
tools.notes: ImageCollage packs differently sized images into a rectangle automatically.

tools.name: ImageCompose
tools.description: Overlays one image on top of another at a given position, respecting alpha channels and optional per-pixel opacity. It is the standard tool for watermarks, annotations and layered composites. Blending functions can be supplied for special effects.

tools.name: ImageCollage
tools.description: Packs a collection of images into a single rectangular collage, optionally sizing each by an associated weight. It handles differently shaped images automatically. Use it for visual summaries of image sets and cluster results.
tools.usage:
ImageCollage[{im1, im2, ...}]
ImageCollage[{w1 -> im1, w2 -> im2, ...}, opts]
tools.example:
imgs = ExampleData[{"TestImage", #}] & /@ {"Lena", "Boat", "Mandrill", "House", "Moon"};
ImageCollage[imgs, Background -> Black, ImagePadding -> 4]

tools.name: ImageChannels
tools.description: Returns the number of color channels in an image, such as 1 for grayscale and 3 for RGB. It is the quickest way to branch code on image type. Pair it with ImageColorSpace for full information.

tools.name: ColorSeparate
tools.description: Splits an image into a list of single-channel images, optionally after converting to another color space. It is the standard way to analyze or process channels independently. Use ColorCombine to put them back together.

tools.name: ColorCombine
tools.description: Builds a multi-channel image from a list of single-channel images, in a specified color space. It is the inverse of ColorSeparate. Use it after per-channel processing or to visualize three scalar fields as one color image.
tools.usage:
ColorCombine[{im1, im2, im3}]
ColorCombine[{im1, im2, im3}, "space"]

tools.name: ImageType
tools.description: Gives the numeric type used to store pixel values, such as "Byte", "Bit16" or "Real32". Conversion happens implicitly in many operations, so checking the type helps explain precision loss. Set the type explicitly when constructing an Image.

tools.name: ImageMeasurements
tools.description: Computes global measurements of an image such as mean intensity, standard deviation, entropy, total intensity and range. A list of property names returns several measurements at once. Use it for quality metrics and quick statistical summaries.

tools.name: ImageValue
tools.description: Returns the pixel value at one or more image coordinates, interpolating between pixels when the position is not integral. Coordinates follow the image convention with the origin at the bottom left. Use it to sample intensities along a path or at detected features.

tools.name: ImagePartition
tools.description: Splits an image into a grid of equally sized tiles, with optional overlap. It returns a nested list of images that can be processed independently and reassembled with ImageAssemble. Use it for block-wise analysis and patch extraction for machine learning.

tools.name: Thumbnail
tools.description: Produces a small preview version of an image, graphic or file, bounded by a maximum size. It preserves aspect ratio and can add a frame or background. Use it for galleries and dataset previews.

tools.name: RemoveBackground
tools.description: Separates the foreground subject of an image from its background, returning the foreground with transparency. Hints such as points, rectangles or a mask can guide the segmentation. Use it for object extraction and compositing.
tools.notes: For finer control over the mask use ImageForestingComponents or WatershedComponents with explicit markers.

tools.name: CurrentImage
tools.description: Captures a frame, or a list of frames, from a connected camera. It is the entry point for live image acquisition inside a notebook. Device selection and image size can be specified.
tools.notes: Requires a camera and, in some environments, permission to access it. $ImagingDevices lists available cameras.
